metadata.title: WEE1 Stabilizes MYC to Promote Therapeutic Resistance in Esophageal Adenocarcinoma

sections.text: Esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) is an aggressive malignancy with poor patient outcomes and limited therapeutic options. WEE1, a G2/M checkpoint kinase, is often upregulated in cancers and associated with resistance to therapy. In this study, we identify a previously unrecognized cytoplasmic role of WEE1 in stabilizing the oncogenic transcription factor MYC and promoting drug resistance in EAC. WEE1 was found to be aberrantly overexpressed and mislocalized to the cytoplasm in EAC cell lines and patient samples. WEE1 depletion or inhibition by MK-1775 significantly reduced MYC protein levels and transcriptional activity by promoting proteasome-mediated degradation. Mechanistically, WEE1 inhibition activated GSK3β, leading to phosphorylation of MYC at threonine 58 and subsequent ubiquitin-dependent degradation. In contrast, overexpression of wild-type WEE1, but not a kinase-dead mutant (K328A), increased p-CDC2 (Y15) and MYC protein levels, confirming that WEE1’s kinase activity is essential for maintaining MYC stability. WEE1 inhibition also downregulated the MYC–ABCC1 axis, decreased MRP1 expression, and impaired drug efflux. A high-throughput screen of 892 FDA-approved compounds identified the histone deacetylase inhibitor Panobinostat as a potent synergistic partner of MK-1775. Combination treatment induced robust apoptosis and markedly suppressed tumor growth in EAC organoids and patient-derived xenograft models. These findings reveal a novel cytoplasmic function of WEE1 in sustaining MYC stability and chemoresistance. Targeting WEE1 destabilizes MYC and enhances therapeutic response, supporting the combination of MK-1775 and Panobinostat as a promising treatment strategy for EAC.

Esophageal Cancer (EC) is the 7 th most diagnosed cancer worldwide, with esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) being the dominant subtype of EC in Western countries [ 1 ]. According to the American Cancer Society, in 2025, an estimated 22,070 new cases of esophageal cancer will be diagnosed in the United States, and 16,250 deaths will result from this disease [ 2 , 3 ]. The 5-year overall survival rate for patients with EAC remains below 25%, and its incidence has continued to rise over the past three decades [ 4 ]. According to the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) Program of the National Cancer Institute, the 5-year relative survival rate for EAC between 2014 and 2020 is approximately 22%. Despite advances in multimodal therapies, the prognosis remains poor, as most patients eventually develop drug resistance that leads to disease progression and distant metastasis [ 5 ]. Therefore, new therapeutic strategies are urgently needed to improve patient outcomes. The G2/M checkpoint kinase WEE1 plays a critical role in maintaining genomic stability by deactivating CDC2, thereby inducing G2 cell cycle arrest and allowing time for DNA damage repair [ 6 ]. Inhibition of WEE1 disrupts this checkpoint control, forcing cells into premature mitosis and leading to uncontrolled cell division and ‘mitotic catastrophe’ [ 7 ]. In cancer cells, various forms of DNA damage activate WEE1 through the ATR/CHK1 signaling pathway, which suppresses CDC2 activity to delay mitotic entry and promote DNA repair [ 8 ]. Notably, WEE1 is frequently upregulated in multiple cancer types and is associated with poor overall survival [ 9 – 11 ]. Because of its key function in regulating the G2/M checkpoint, targeting WEE1 has been proposed as an effective strategy to sensitize tumors to chemotherapy and radiotherapy [ 12 – 15 ]. Furthermore, analysis of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) data identified TP53 mutations in approximately 71% of EAC cases [ 16 ]. Given that TP53 loss compromises the G1 checkpoint, EAC cells may become dependent on the G2/M checkpoint for survival, making them particularly susceptible to WEE1 inhibition [ 17 (67)]. Overall, inhibition of WEE1 forces cancer cells to enter mitosis with incompletely replicated DNA, resulting in mitotic catastrophe and subsequent cell death [ 18 ]. The multifunctional transcription factor c-MYC is implicated in various cellular processes, including transcription, cell survival, proliferation, and metabolism [ 19 – 21 ]. It is found to be dysregulated in approximately 70% of Human cancers (Pelengaris S, 2002) [ 22 (68)]. Elevated levels of C-MYC protein have been noted in 50% of Barette’s metaplasia and 90% of EAC [ 23 ]. Currently, pharmacological targeting of C-MYC has been far from clinical use due to various factors, including its predominant nuclear localization, ‘undruggable’ protein structure, lack of ligand-binding sites, and large protein–protein interaction surfaces [ 20 , 24 ]. Due to these challenges, targeting C-MYC has been largely focused on indirect approaches, such as suppressing C-MYC transcription/translation, as well as destabilization [ 25 , 26 ]. Selective degradation of C-MYC by hijacking the ubiquitin-proteasome machinery can be regarded as an ideal approach [ 27 ]. The N-terminal phosphorylation of T58 in C-MYC, mediated by GSK3β, is critical for its recognition by the ubiquitin-proteasome system and subsequent degradation [ 28 ]. Cells deploy diverse strategies to ensure strict regulation of C-MYC abundance and activity [ 29 (69)]. Several Ubiquitin ligases (E3s) have been identified as key regulators of C-MYC degradation [ 30 – 32 ]. Among them, the best-characterized is the Cullin-ring Ubiquitin ligase complex containing the substrate recognition subunit Fbxw7 (CRL1 FBXW7 ). The stability of C-MYC is controlled by this complex in a phosphorylation-dependent manner, requiring phosphorylation of C-MYC at threonine 58 (T58) by GSK3β. This phosphorylation creates a recognition site for FBXW7-mediated ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation (26). Notably, mutations at the T58 site are common in many cancers and increase C-MYC stability [ 33 , 34 ]. Supporting this, transgenic mice expressing a C-MYC T58A mutant develop tumors more rapidly and at a higher frequency than those expressing the wild-type protein [ 33 , 34 ]. Similarly, conditional deletion of Fbxw7 in the mouse thymus led to C-MYC accumulation and aggressive thymic lymphomas. Moreover, CRL1 FBXW7 -dependent C-MYC degradation is essential for maintaining normal stemness, including that of hematopoietic stem cells, keratinocytes, and cancer stem cells [ 35 (70)]. Chemoresistance in cancer arises from multiple mechanisms, one of the most prominent being the altered expression of ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters. These membrane proteins actively transport a wide range of physiological substrates—including prostaglandins, eicosanoids, steroids, and chemotherapeutic drugs—across cellular membranes in an ATP-dependent manner [ 36 , 37 ]. To date, 48 functional ABC transporter genes have been identified and categorized into 7 subfamilies (A to G) [ 38 ]. Nearly half of all human cancers overexpress P-glycoprotein (P-gp), which contributes to drug resistance by reducing intracellular drug accumulation through enhanced efflux [ 39 ]. Over-expression of ABC transporter genes, including ABCB1, ABCC1, and ABCG2, is a well-known cause of reduced drug accumulation within tumor cells, promoting drug resistance [ 40 (71)]. Both MYCN and C-MYC have been shown to transcriptionally regulate multiple ABC transporters, either activating or repressing their expression depending on the cellular context [ 41 ]. Consequently, stabilization of c-MYC promotes the expression of drug-efflux pumps, such as ABCC1, further enhancing resistance to chemotherapy. In this study, we uncover a previously unrecognized role of WEE1 in reinforcing C-MYC–driven oncogenic functions by suppressing GSK3β activity, thereby stabilizing C-MYC in EAC. We identified the critical role of the WEE1–C-MYC axis in promoting the survival of esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) cells. Inhibition of WEE1 using MK-1775 leads to C-MYC degradation, resulting in a marked reduction in cell viability. Furthermore, through FDA-approved drug screening, we identify Panobinostat as a potent therapeutic agent that synergized with WEE1 inhibition, providing a strong rationale for combining these drugs as a novel therapeutic strategy against C-MYC–driven EAC.

Immortalized non-cancerous esophageal cell line EPC2, Human Barette’s esophagus cell lines BAR-T, CPA, and CPB were acquired as mentioned before [ 42 ] and cultured in complete epithelial medium (Cell Biologics, Chicago, IL). EAC cell lines FLO1, OE33, OE19, and ESO 26 were obtained as reported before Ref ( 37 ) and cultured in DMEM or RPMI (Gibco, Waltham, MA) supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco) and 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin (Gibco). All the cell lines were grown at 37°C in 5% CO 2 incubator. Cell line authentication was done at Labcorp (Burlington, NC) using short tandem repeat profiling. They were routinely monitored for mycoplasma contamination using the Mycoplasma detection kit (Southern Biotech, Birmingham, AL). WEE1 and p-CDC2 Y15 antibodies were purchased from Santa Cruz Biotechnology (Dallas, TX). C-MYC, p-C-MYC T58, P-GSK3β S9, GSK3β, PARP, CL-PARP, Caspase 3, Cl-Caspase 3, HA tag, CD133, SOX9, SOX2, CD44, OCT4, Nanog and Ki-67 antibodies were obtained from Cell Signaling Technologies (Danvers, MA). The MRP1 antibody was purchased from Abcam (Cambridge, MA). β-Actin antibody was obtained from Sigma Aldrich (St. Louis, MO), and HRP-conjugated anti-Rabbit and anti-Mouse antibodies were purchased from Promega (Madison, WI). MK-1775, Oxaliplatin, Cisplatin, and Panobinostat were supplied by Selleck Chemicals (Houston, TX). Cycloheximide and MG132 were obtained from Sigma Aldrich.

Immunohistochemical staining for WEE1 was performed on twenty human esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) tissue samples as mentioned before (37). Digital image analysis was conducted using CellProfiler software (version 4.2.1; Broad Institute, Cambridge, MA, USA) on three randomly selected EAC samples, analyzing over 1,000 individual cells. WEE1 expression was quantified separately in the nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments. Color deconvolution was applied to separate the hematoxylin (nuclear) and DAB (WEE1-positive) channels. Nuclear and cytoplasmic regions were segmented using intensity-based thresholding, allowing for precise quantification of WEE1 expression levels in each cellular compartment across all analyzed tissues.

Cell fractionation in FLO1 and OE33 cell lines was carried out according to the protocol described in the Cell Fractionation Kit (CST). Cells were trypsinized and washed in cold 1X PBS. The cell pellet was resuspended in 0.5 mL of cold 1X PBS, and 100 μL of it was used as Whole Cell Lysate (WCL). The remaining aliquot was centrifuged at 500g for 5 min at 4°C. The supernatant was aspirated, and the pellet was resuspended in 500μl of CIB (Cytoplasmic Isolation Buffer) and vortexed for 5 seconds. The suspension was incubated on ice for 5 minutes and then centrifuged for 5 minutes at 500g. The supernatant was saved as the cytoplasmic fraction. The pellet was resuspended in 500 μL of MIB (Membrane Isolation Buffer) and vortexed for 15 seconds, followed by incubation on ice for 5 minutes. Then the suspension was centrifuged for 5 min at 8000g, and the supernatant was saved as the Membrane and organelle fraction. Finally, the pellet was resuspended in 250 μL of CyNIB (Cytoskeletal/Nuclear Isolation buffer) and sonicated for 5 seconds and then saved as the Cytoskeletal and Nuclear fraction. Each fraction, along with WCL, was resolved in a 10% SDS-PAGE gel and transferred to a Nitrocellulose membrane and probed for WEE1, P84, and α-Tubulin.

0.1ml of cold RIPA buffer (SCBT) was added to cells grown in 6-well plates (2 x 10 5 cells/well), then scraped using a cell scraper. The cell suspension was sonicated and centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 10 minutes at 4 °C. The supernatant was transferred to new tubes, and the protein concentration of the cell lysates was estimated using the BCA kit (Pierce Biotechnology, Waltham, MA). 10μg of the protein lysates were subjected to SDS-PAGE, and the protein bands were transferred to a Nitrocellulose membrane (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA). Membranes were blocked in 5% BSA containing TBS-T for 1 hour, then probed with the specific primary antibody at 4 °C overnight. On the following day, the membranes were washed for 5 minutes with TBS-T thrice, then incubated with Anti-Mouse/Anti-Rabbit secondary antibodies for 2 hours. Membranes were washed as before, and the protein bands were detected using chemiluminescence substrates (Millipore, Billerica, MA) in the GelDoc Go (Bio-Rad) Gel documentation system.

FLO1, OE33 and SK-GT4 cell lines were treated with MK-1775 (FLO1: 75nM – 1.17nM, OE33: 500nM – 7.81nM, SK-GT4: 300nM – 4.68nM & OE19: 800 nM – 12.5nM) and Panobinostat (FLO1: 25nM – 0.39 nM, OE33: 35 nM – 0.54n M, SK-GT4: 50 nM – 0.78nM & OE19: 20nM – 0.31 nM) for 8 x 8 Synergy ATP Glow assay as reported in our previous publication [ 42 ]. For IC50 determination, FLO1, OE33, OE19 & SK-GT4 cells were seeded at a density of 1500 cells/well in a total volume of 100μl of 10% FBS containing DMEM / RPMI in a 96-well plate and treated with MK-1775 (1μM – 0.01 μM) or Panobinostat (0.5μM – 0.07μM) for 96 hours. For determining the synergy between Oxaliplatin and MK 1775, 20μM Oxaliplatin was used as top concentration and 1μM MK1775 was used as top concentration. For determining the synergy between Cisplatin and MK 1775, 20μM Cisplatin was used as top concentration and 1μM MK1775 was used as top concentration. Cell viability was determined using the Cell Titer-Glo reagent (Promega, Madison, WI) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The luminescence signals were detected in a FluOStar microplate reader (BMG Labtech, Ortenberg, Germany), and the IC50 Values were determined through the Log (Inhibitor) Vs Response (4 parameter) model using Graphpad Prism software

sections.section: Dna/Rna Transfection And Luciferase Reporter Activity Assay
sections.text: siRNA transfection was performed using Lipojet transfection reagent (Signagen Laboratories, Fredrick, MD) as per the manufacturer’s instructions. 80 picomoles of WEE1 siRNA #1 and WEE1 siRNA #2, 40pM and 80pM of MYC siRNA were transfected into 2.5 x 10 5 cells per well in a 6-well plate. The medium was changed after 6 hours of transfection, and the cells were harvested 48 hours later. For luciferase reporter assay, 0.5 μg of 4X EMS luciferase reporter plasmid (Stephen R Hann, University of Colorado, Aurora, CO) was co-transfected with 0.1μg of Renilla luciferase plasmid with or without 0.5μg pWZL Blast C-MYC plasmid (Addgene plasmid #10674, Watertown, MA) into 2.5 x 10 5 cells/well in a 6-well plate using Polyjet (Signagen). The media was changed after 6 hours of transfection, and the cells were harvested after 48 hours in passive lysis buffer. The Luciferase reporter activity was determined using the Dual Luciferase Reporter Assay System (Promega) and a FluOSTAR 96-well plate reader (BMG Labtech). The results were expressed as mean ± SD, and statistical significance between the treated and untreated control groups was calculated using one-way ANOVA with GraphPad Prism software. WEE1 K328A mutation was generated using Quick-change Lightning site-directed Mutagenesis kit (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA) as per the manufacturer's instructions. For WEE1 over expression, pCMV6-XL4-WEE1 (Origene, sc117999, Rockville, MD) at a concentration of 0.05 μg and 0.1 μg was transfected using Polyjet transfection reagent in a 6-well plate as described above. 0.1μg of pCMV-XL4 plasmid was used as control in this experiment. For WEE1 over expression followed by MK 1775 treatment, OE33 cells were transfected with 0.2μg, 0.4μg and 0.5μg of pCMV6-XL4-WEE1 and 0.5 μg of pCMV-XL4 control plasmid for 24 Hours. The transfected cells were treated with 1μM concentration of MK 1775 whereas the untreated cells served as control.

To determine the interaction between GSK3β and MYC proteins with or without MK-1775 treatment, we performed PLA using the Duolink in situ Red Starter kit for Mouse/Rabbit (Sigma-Aldrich). OE19, OE33, and SK-GT4 cells were seeded in an 8-well chamber slide at a density of 5000 cells/chamber. The next day, the cells were treated with/ without a 1 μM concentration of MK-1775 for 24 Hours and then fixed with a fresh 4% PFA solution for 20 minutes at room temperature. They were washed with cold PBS three times. 0.1 % Triton-X-100 (Sigma) in PBS was used for permeabilizing the cells for 10 min, followed by three washes in PBS. The cells were blocked in a 5% BSA solution for 60 min at room temperature and then incubated with primary antibodies for GSK3β (Mouse) and MYC (Rabbit) in a humidified chamber overnight at 4°C. The following day, primary antibodies were washed from the chamber slide according to the manufacturer’s protocol and incubated with the Oligo nucleotide conjugated anti-Rabbit and anti-Mouse secondary antibodies (Duolink In Situ PLA probe antiMouse Minus and Anti-Rabbit Plus, Sigma) in antibody diluent. The slides were incubated in a pre-heated humidity chamber for 1 hour at 37°C. Slides were washed twice for 5 minutes each in wash buffer A. The ligase solution was added to the slides and incubated for 30 min at 37°C. Slides were washed twice and incubated with polymerase-containing amplification solution for 100 minutes at 37°C. Finally, the cells were washed in buffer B twice, air dried, and mounted in DAPI-containing mounting medium. Fluorescence was imaged in Zeiss LSM Confocal microscope (Dublin, CA).

To establish organoids from PDX, a portion of the subcutaneous PDX tumor was extracted and minced. The segments were digested in 10 mL of Gland digestion media containing 5 mg/mL of Collagenase A (Stem Cell Technologies, Vancouver, Canada) and 6.5 mg/mL of Dispase II (Sigma-Aldrich) in DMEM containing 20 mM HEPES, 0.2% FBS, and 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin. The PDX tissue was agitated by gentle inversion for 40 minutes at 37°C and centrifuged at 100g for 5 minutes. The supernatant containing connective tissue was aspirated, and the pellet was rinsed in gland rinse media (DMEM containing 0.5 mM DTT) and then centrifuged at 100g for 5 minutes. The pellet was incubated in 2ml of pre-warmed TrypLE Express (Gibco) at 37°C for 4 minutes with gentle agitation in between. Digestion was stopped by adding 2ml of PBS containing 0.2% FBS. Sequentially, the suspension was passed through 40μM cell strainer (Argos Technologies, Vernon Hills, IL) and centrifuged at 1200 rpm for 5 min. The pellet was resuspended in a Matrigel matrix (Corning, Corning, NY) and cultured in Organoid Growth Medium (Stem Cell Technologies) for 7 days. MK-1775 treatment (2 μM) and Panobinostat treatment (0.1 μM) were given for 3 days. The diameter of the organoids was measured using Infinity Software (Teledyne Lumenera, Ontario, Canada) and expressed as the mean ± SD. Statistical significance between the treated groups and the untreated control was calculated using one-way ANOVA in Graph-pad prism software

2.5 x 10 5 OE33 and OE19 cells were cultured in 6-well plates and treated for 24 hours with MK-1775 alone (2 μM for OE19 & 1 μM for OE33) or in combination with Panobinostat (25 nM for OE33 and 0.1 μM for OE19). Annexin V and Sytox Red (Invitrogen, Waltham, MA) dual staining was performed using FITC Annexin V apoptosis detection kit (BioLegend, San Diego, CA). Cells were collected and stained according to the Manufacturer’s instructions. Sytox red was used instead of PI at a concentration of 0.2μM and analyzed in FACS Aria Fusion (BD, Franklin Lakes, NJ) at the Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center’s (SCCC) Flow Cytometry Shared Resources (FCSR). The FCS files were analyzed using FCS Express 7 Software (Pasadena, CA). Annexin V-stained cells in each group were expressed as a percentage of apoptosis, and statistical significance between the treated groups and the untreated control was calculated using One-way ANOVA in GraphPad Prism software.

Total RNA was isolated using Trizol reagent (Ambion, Waltham, MA). 2μg of total RNA was used for reverse transcription using High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Applied Biosystems, Waltham, MA) as per the manufacturer’s instructions. qRT-PCR reaction was performed using primers ordered from Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT, Coralville, IA) and SYBR green from Abclonal (Woburn, MA). The sequences of the qRT-PCR primers are included in Supplementary Table 1. The qRT-PCR reaction was run in the Bio-Rad CFX Connect Real-time system with the conditions specified by the CFX Manager Software Version 3.0. The expression level of the target genes was normalized to HPRT1. The mRNA expression levels were analyzed using the formula 2 (RT-Et) / 2 (Rn-En) as previously described [ 43 ]. The significance between the untreated and MK-1775-treated groups was determined using an unpaired t-test with GraphPad Prism software. RNA sequencing was performed in FLO1 and OE33 cell lines treated with control and WEE1 siRNA as described in [ 42 , 44 ].

GEJ085-01A gastroesophageal junction tumor tissue microarray consisting of 80 late-stage adenocarcinoma cases and 5 matched normal tissue cores was purchased from US Biolabs (Germantown, MD). An H&E-stained TMA slide was used to verify the histology of the tissues. The IF in cell lines was performed as reported before [ 45 ]. For paraffin-embedded tissue sections, deparaffinization was performed three times (3 minutes each) in xylene (Sigma), followed by incubation in 100% ethanol (Spectrum Chemicals, New Brunswick, NJ) twice, each for 2 minutes. The slides were then sequentially incubated in 95% ethanol, 75% ethanol, 50% ethanol, and deionized water for 2 minutes each. Antigen retrieval was performed in TE buffer (pH 9, Invitrogen) by initially boiling the buffer in a microwave. The slides were placed in the heated TE buffer and steamed for 20 minutes. The sections were cooled down to room temperature and washed in water, followed by PBS. The sections were permeabilized in 0.1% Triton-X-100 containing PBS for 10 minutes and blocked with 10% goat serum (Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA) for 1 hour. Slides were washed in PBS-T thrice and further blocked in 5% BSA containing PBS-T and then incubated with primary antibodies WEE1 at 1:50 dilution, C-MYC at 1:100 dilution, p-CDC2 Y15 at 1:100 dilution, MRP1 at 1:50 dilution, and Ki67 at 1:100 dilution, overnight at 4°C in a moist chamber. After washing the slides in PBS-T three times, the slides were incubated with anti-Mouse AF 488 and Anti-Rabbit AF 565 Conjugated secondary antibodies (Invitrogen) at a dilution of 1:400 in the dark for 2 hours. Finally, the slides were washed in PBS-T three times, air-dried, and mounted in Vectashield mounting medium (Newark, CA). The images were acquired using a Zeiss LSM Confocal Microscope with Airyscan 2 (Zeiss) at the Imaging facility of FCSR at SCCC. For quantitative analysis of immunofluorescence (IF) staining, single-cell image analysis was performed using CellProfiler software (Broad Institute, Cambridge, MA). Individual nuclei were identified based on DAPI staining, and corresponding cytoplasmic or nuclear fluorescence intensities for target proteins (e.g., WEE1, and C-MYC) were measured within each segmented cell. Background fluorescence was subtracted, and mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) values were calculated for all detected cells. The resulting single-cell data were exported to Excel and GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA) for statistical analysis and visualization, enabling precise quantification of protein expression levels and correlation analysis.

Untreated and MK-1775-treated OE33 and OE19 cells were fixed and stained with PI as reported before [ 46 ]. Untreated and MK-1775-treated OE33 and OE19 cells were harvested 24 Hours after the treatment and fixed in cold ethanol for 48 hours. The fixed cells were washed twice in PBS and then subjected to RNase A treatment (Sigma Aldrich) for 30 minutes at 37 °C. Finally, the fixed cells were stained with PI (1 mg/mL) in 0.1% Triton X-100 containing PBS. Cell cycle distribution in various phases was analyzed in FACS Aria Fusion (BD Biosciences) at the FCSR of SCCC. Cell cycle distribution in various phases was analyzed using FCS Express 7 software and represented as Mean ± SD values. Significance between the control and MK-1775 treated groups was calculated through an unpaired T-test using Graphpad Prism software

Flow cytometry was used to determine the accumulation of intracellular Rhodamine 123 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Dallas, TX in OE33 and SK-GT4 cell lines. Cells were cultured with or without a 1μM concentration of MK-1775 for 24 Hours. A 0.25 μM concentration of Rhodamine 123 was added to the cells and incubated for 60 minutes at 37°C in a CO 2 incubator. To determine the influx, cells were washed twice in PBS, trypsinized, and resuspended in 1% BSA-containing PBS, then subjected to FACS analysis. To determine efflux, cells in duplicate plates, as treated above, were washed twice in PBS, then incubated in RPMI containing 10% FBS for 4 hours in a CO 2 incubator. Subsequently, the cells were harvested and analyzed for the intracellular accumulation of Rhodamine 123 using a Cytoflex flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA). The percentage of Rhodamine 123 retained within the cells was calculated by dividing the Mean Fluorescence Intensity (MFI) of the influx by the MFI of the efflux and multiplying by 100. Results were expressed as Mean ± SD values, and the significance between the untreated control and MK-1775-treated cells was determined using an unpaired t-test.

Untreated / MK-1775-treated cells were subjected to cycloheximide (Sigma Aldrich) treatment (10μg/ml) and harvested at specific time intervals. Cells were then lysed in RIPA buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors and subjected to SDS-PAGE followed by western blot for C-MYC, β-Actin, and WEE1. The intensity of the C-MYC bands was quantified using Image Lab software (Bio-Rad) and normalized to the intensity of the β-Actin band. The half-life of C-MYC was then determined through linear regression analysis in GraphPad Prism software (Boston, MA).

Recombinant full length WEE1 (Millipore-Sigma) at a concentration of 0.01μg to 0.1μg and GSK3ß (Thermo Fisher) at a concentration of 0.05μg was used for the kinase assay. Recombinant S100A4 was used as negative control. Kinase reaction was set up to a final volume of 20μl in kinase assay buffer (HEPES 50mM pH 7.4, Mgcl2 3mM, Mncl2 3mM, DTT 1mM, Sodium orthovanadate 3μM and 0.5mM ATP). The tubes were incubated at 30°C for 30 minutes and stopped after the addition of SDS-PAGE sample loading buffer. The reactions were resolved by SDS-PAGE followed by Western blot detection of P-GSK3ß S9, GSK3ß, WEE1 and S100A4.

For ubiquitination assay, OE33 cells were seeded at a density of 1X10 6 cells per 10cm dish and transfected with 3μg concentration of HA-Ubiquitin plasmid and 2μg of pWZ-Plast-MYC using Polyjet transfection reagent. After 24 Hours of transfection, 1μM concentration of MK 1775 was added to the plates and incubated for 24 Hours. Cells were washed in ice-cold PBS and lysed in RIPA buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Lysates were sonicated and centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 10 min at 4°C and subjected to immunoprecipitation with Rabbit IgG (control) and Rabbit anti-MYC antibody. The immunoprecipitate’s were resolved in SDS-PAGE and probed using Anti-HA antibody in Western blot.

sections.section: Drug Screening And Drug Combination Analysis
sections.text: To identify drugs that synergize with MK1775, we utilized a compound library from Cayman Chemicals (Ann Arbor, MI) for a high-throughput drug screen of 892 FDA-approved compounds. In the first round of screening, the OE19 cell line (relatively resistant to MK-1775) was seeded at a density of 1000 cells/well in 96-well plates and incubated with a 0.5 μM concentration of MK-1775 in combination with a 1 μM concentration of FDA-approved drugs from the library for 96 hours. Cell viability was assessed using the ATP Glow assay (Promega), and drug interactions were analyzed using Bliss synergy score analysis [ 47 (72)]. Compounds showing a significant reduction in cell viability for the combination group compared to either MK-1775 or the drug alone (P < 0.05) were considered positive hits, yielding 21 candidates. These hits were further evaluated in a second round of screening using FLO1 and SK-GT4 cell lines to identify the most synergistic combinations.

The IACUC of the University of Miami has approved animal work (protocol #: IPROTO202100000099). Human EAC PDX were acquired and generated in Mice as reported before [ 48 (66)]. When the tumor size reached approximately 150 mm 3 , Mice were randomized into 4 groups 1. Control 2. MK-1775 treatment alone 3. Panobinostat treatment alone and 4. Combination of MK-1775 and Panobinostat treatment. Tumor volume and mouse weight were recorded twice a week for a period of 4 weeks. MK-1775 (Selleckchem, Houston, TX) was administered at a dose of 25 mg/kg three times a week through Oral gavage. Panobinostat (Selleckchem) was administered intraperitonially at a dose of 10 mg/kg, once a week for 4 weeks. Tumor volume was calculated using the formula Volume = (long dimension) x (short dimension) 2 . Tumor growth was monitored for four weeks and plotted as tumor size (mm 3 , mean ± SD) versus time (days) using GraphPad Prism software. The maximal tumor size permitted by the University of Miami IACUC protocol was 1,000 mm 3 , and this limit was not exceeded in any of the experimental animals. For the determination of PARP, cl-PARP, Caspase 3, and Cl-Caspase 3 using Western blot, a small portion of the Mice PDX tumor tissue was homogenized with RIPA buffer in Green 1.5ml snap-cap GATOR ™ Tubes (Next Advance, NY) at 4°C in a Bullet blender (Next Advance, NY) for 10 minutes, set at a speed of 6. The tissue lysate was centrifuged at 1200 rpm for 10 minutes at 4°C, and the protein concentration of the supernatant was estimated using the BCA kit (Pierce Biotechnology). For the quantification of P-CDC2 Y15, C-MYC, MRP1, and Ki67 using immunofluorescence, a portion of PDX tumor tissue (immediately after harvest) was fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin (Sigma-Aldrich) for 24 hours in Histology cassettes (VWR, Radnor, PA) followed by paraffin embedding and sectioning at the CMSR of SCCC. The histology of the tissue sections was verified through H&E staining before proceeding with IF staining, and CellProfiler software was used to quantify the fluorescence signals. The intensity of the fluorescence signals from the MK-1775, PANO, and Combination treatment groups was compared with that of the vehicle-treated control group using one-way ANOVA, and the results were expressed as mean ± SD using GraphPad Prism software.
Quantitative values are expressed as Mean ± SD. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and Student’s t-test were used to evaluate statistical significance in GraphPad Prism (San Diego, CA).

sections.section: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (Gsea) And Mrna Expression Analysis For Human Eac Samples.
sections.text: Gene expression datasets for esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) ( GSE26886 , GSE37200 , GSE37201 , and GSE74553 ) and the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database. For each dataset, samples were divided into WEE1-high and WEE1-low groups based on the median expression of WEE1 . GSEA was performed in R (version 4.3.1) using the clusterProfiler (version 4.10.0) and enrichplot (version 1.22.0) packages, with the Hallmark (h.all.v7.5.1.symbols.gmt) and C2 curated gene sets from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB) as reference pathways. The signal-to-noise ratio ranked genes, and enrichment scores were calculated using 1,000 phenotype permutations. Normalized enrichment scores (NES), nominal P -values, and false discovery rate (FDR) q -values were computed to identify significantly enriched pathways. Visualization of enrichment plots and heatmaps was performed using ggplot2 (v3.5.1) and pheatmap (v1.0.12) packages. Additionally, the differential expression of WEE1 and MYC mRNA in normal versus tumor tissues was analyzed using the TNMplot online tool ( https://tnmplot.com/ ), which integrates data from the TCGA, GTEx, and GEO repositories.

sections.section: Wee1 Overexpression Correlates With C-Myc In Esophageal Adenocarcinoma
sections.text: Our previous publication demonstrated that WEE1 is overexpressed in esophageal adenocarcinoma and promotes chemotherapy resistance through smoking-induced miRNA dysregulation (37). In this study, we further demonstrate that WEE1, a classically nuclear kinase, is aberrantly overexpressed in the cytoplasm of EAC cells. Initially, we performed IHC staining for WEE1 in EAC tissue sections, followed by quantitative single-cell image analysis using CellProfiler ( Supplementary Figure 1A ), which revealed predominant cytoplasmic localization ( Fig. 1A & 1B ). To further prove the cytosolic sequestration of WEE1 within EAC cells, we performed Cell fractionation in FLO1 and OE33 cell lines to enrich the proteins in various cellular compartments, followed by a Western blot for WEE1. The purity of the Nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions was verified using P84 as well as α-tubulin, respectively. The results confirmed the cytosolic localization of WEE1 protein, aligning with the IHC results ( Fig. 1C ). Moreover, IF imaging revealed the cytoplasmic localization of WEE1 and the nuclear localization of C-MYC in both EAC cell lines, FLO1 and OE33, further confirming previous data. ( Fig. 1D ). To explore the biological significance of this cytosolic WEE1 expression, we performed gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) by comparing WEE1-high and WEE1-low EAC tumors across four GEO datasets ( GSE26886 , GSE37200 , GSE37201 , and GSE74553 ) and the TCGA EAC cohort. The analysis revealed strong enrichment of C-MYC signaling pathways in WEE1-high tumors ( P < 0.0001 ), suggesting that WEE1 may regulate oncogenic MYC activity ( Fig. 1E & IF ). Using the TNMplot online tool, we further confirmed that both WEE1 and MYC mRNA levels were significantly elevated in esophageal cancer tissues compared with normal esophagus (Normal, n = 418; Tumor, n = 161) ( Fig. 1G & 1H ). Immunofluorescence (IF) staining of tissue microarrays containing normal esophagus ( n = 5) and gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinomas ( n = 20) further confirmed a strong positive correlation between WEE1 and C-MYC protein expression in EAC ( Fig 1I – 1K ) To further validate the correlation between WEE1 and C-MYC protein levels, WB was performed for WEE1 and C-MYC proteins in Human Normal esophageal cell line -EPC, Non-neoplastic Barette’s epithelial cell lines – CPA, CPB & BAR-T, and EAC cell lines -FLO1, OE33, SK-GT4, OE19 & ESO26. EAC cell lines exhibited relatively high WEE1 and C-MYC proteins compared to the non-cancerous cell lines ( Supplementary Figure 1B ). The above finding confirms the over-expression of WEE1 and C-MYC in EAC, which could be closely associated with the progression of EAC from the normal esophagus. Together, these findings demonstrate that WEE1, traditionally known as a nuclear kinase, is aberrantly overexpressed in the cytoplasm of human EAC, where it correlates with MYC activation and may play a distinct oncogenic role in tumor progression.

sections.section: Wee1 Knockdown Or Inhibition Destabilizes C-Myc And Impairs Its Transcriptional Activity
sections.text: Given our observation that WEE1 is aberrantly localized in the cytoplasm of EAC cells, we next sought to determine whether WEE1 regulates C-MYC stability and activity. To investigate this, we first silenced WEE1 using siRNA in EAC cell lines OE33, SK-GT4, and OE19. To confirm the specificity of WEE1 knock-down, we further used a different pool of WEE1 siRNA #2 ( Supplementary Figure 2A & 2B ). WEE1 knockdown led to a marked reduction in phosphorylation of CDC2 at Y15, a known downstream target of WEE1 [ 49 (73)], along with a significant decrease in C-MYC protein levels across all tested cell lines ( Fig. 2A ). Next, we checked MYC mRNA level following WEE1 knock-down / inhibition and the results suggested that protein stability is not the only mechanism that regulate MYC level. Both transcriptional regulation and protein stability works cooperatively ( Supplementary Figure 2C & 2D ). Flow cytometric analysis showed that WEE1 depletion induced G2/M arrest, with the proportion of cells in G2/M phase increasing from 21.5% in control siRNA-transfected OE19 cells to 33.4% in WEE1 siRNA-transfected cells ( Fig. 2B and 2C ) as expected. To assess whether WEE1 depletion affects C-MYC transcriptional function, we performed a luciferase reporter assay using a construct containing four tandem E-box (EMS) elements responsive to C-MYC [ 50 (74)]. WEE1 knockdown markedly reduced C-MYC–driven luciferase activity, indicating impaired transcriptional activity ( Fig. 2D ). In this experiment, C-MYC overexpression was included as a positive control and strongly enhanced luciferase reporter activity as expected. Notably, WEE1 siRNA significantly reduced this C-MYC overexpression–induced luciferase activity across all three tested EAC cell lines, further confirming that WEE1 is required to sustain C-MYC transcriptional function ( Fig. 2D ). Consistently, qRT-PCR analysis revealed that expression of C-MYC target genes, including MNT, CDK4, and ABCC1, was significantly decreased upon WEE1 silencing in OE33 and OE19 cells ( Fig. 2E ). Immunofluorescence staining further confirmed that WEE1 knockdown reduced C-MYC staining in SK-GT4 and OE33 cells ( Fig. 2F ), consistent with the observed decrease in protein expression. Furthermore, RNA sequencing analysis of OE33 cells revealed that WEE1 siRNA knockdown significantly downregulated the HALLMARK_MYC_TARGETS_V1 and HALLMARK_MYC_TARGETS_V2 gene sets compared with control cells, further supporting that WEE1 is essential for sustaining C-MYC transcriptional activity ( Fig. 2G & Supplementary Figure 2E ). Next, we pharmacologically inhibited WEE1 using the selective small-molecule inhibitor MK-1775 in the same panel of EAC cell lines. Similar to the siRNA results, MK-1775 treatment reduced CDC2 phosphorylation and suppressed C-MYC protein expression in all cell lines ( Fig. 3A ). Paradoxically, MK-1775 treatment decreased the WEE1 protein levels in OE33 and SK-GT4 cell lines. Knockdown of MYC using siRNA resulted in a reduction of both WEE1 mRNA and protein levels. Further analysis revealed the presence of a MYC binding site in the WEE1 promoter region, creating a feedback loop ( Supplementary Figure 3A – 3D ). Flow cytometry analysis demonstrated an increase in the G2/M population from 15.8% in untreated OE19 cells to 34.7% after MK-1775 treatment, as expected ( Fig. 3B and 3C ). Moreover, MK-1775 significantly decreased C-MYC reporter activity ( Fig. 3D , top panels ), further confirmed through Western blot analysis of C-MYC using cell lysate from the reporter activity assay ( Fig. 3D , bottom panels ) and downregulated key C-MYC target genes such as MNT, CDK4, and ABCC1, consistent with reduced transcriptional activity measured by qRT-PCR analysis ( Fig. 3E ). Immunofluorescence analysis confirmed that WEE1 inhibition using MK-1775 decreased p-CDC2 (Y15) and C-MYC staining FLO1 and OE33 cells as expected, confirming inhibition of WEE1 activity and reduced C-MYC expression level ( Fig. 3F ). Collectively, these results demonstrate that both genetic depletion and pharmacological inhibition of WEE1 decrease C-MYC protein expression level and suppress its transcriptional activity, thereby impairing oncogenic signaling and inducing G2/M arrest in EAC cells.

sections.section: Wee1 Inhibition Promotes Proteasome-Mediated Degradation Of C-Myc
sections.text: We next investigated whether WEE1 inhibition decreased the C-MYC protein level in EAC due to decreased synthesis or enhanced degradation of C-MYC. Since our EAC cell line models did not show a consistent decrease in C-MYC mRNA after WEE1 knockdown or inhibition, we focused on assessing C-MYC protein stability. To determine whether C-MYC is degraded through the proteasome pathway, we evaluated its stability in the presence or absence of the proteasome inhibitor MG132. EAC cell lines (OE19, OE33, and SK-GT4) were treated with MK-1775 (1 μM for OE33, SK-GT4 & 2μM for OE19) for 24 hours, with or without MG132 co-treatment ( Fig. 4A ). Similarly, OE19 and OE33 cells transfected with control or WEE1 siRNA were analyzed under the same conditions ( Fig. 4B ). Because C-MYC is continuously subjected to rapid basal turnover, MG132 treatment inherently led to an accumulation of C-MYC protein in the control cells. Furthermore, MG132 successfully rescued C-MYC protein levels depleted by WEE1 inhibition or knockdown ( Fig. 4A & B ). To confirm the ubiquitin mediated degradation of C-MYC following MK 1775 treatment, we performed ubiquitination assay by over -expressing HA-Ubiquitin and C-MYC in OE33 cell lines. Pull down of C-MYC followed by detection of HA tagged Ubiquitin revealed, a smear of high molecular weight poly-ubiquitinated C-MYC following MK 1775 treatment, compared to the control IgG pull down and MYC pull down from untreated cells ( Supplementary figure 3E ). To further confirm this mechanism, we performed a cycloheximide (CHX) chase assay to determine changes in C-MYC half-life following WEE1 inhibition. CHX, a protein synthesis inhibitor, allows measurement of degradation kinetics over time. EAC cell lines (OE19, OE33, and SK-GT4) were treated with CHX for 0, 10, 30, and 60 minutes after exposure to MK-1775. Compared with control cells, WEE1 inhibition markedly accelerated C-MYC degradation, reducing its half-life to approximately 36.6 minutes in OE19, 35.6 minutes in OE33, and 27.1 minutes in SK-GT4. In contrast, the half-life in control cells exceeded 60 minutes ( Fig. 4C – F ). Taken together, these findings demonstrate that WEE1 activity is essential for maintaining C-MYC protein stability. Inhibition or loss of WEE1 promotes degradation of C-MYC protein, providing a mechanistic explanation for the observed decline in C-MYC levels following WEE1 targeting in EAC cells.

sections.section: Wee1 Inhibition Promotes Gsk3Β-Mediated Phosphorylation And Degradation Of C-Myc
sections.text: Degradation of C-MYC through the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway is known to depend on phosphorylation of threonine 58 (T58) by GSK3β [ 51 ]. To determine whether WEE1 influences this process, we analyzed C-MYC phosphorylation at T58 following either pharmacological inhibition or genetic knockdown of WEE1. In EAC cell lines (OE33, SK-GT4, and OE19) treated with the WEE1 inhibitor MK-1775, the level of phosphorylated T58 C-MYC (p-T58 C-MYC) was markedly increased, while total C-MYC protein levels were substantially reduced. This was accompanied by a decrease in the inhibitory phosphorylation of GSK3β at serine 9 (p-S9 GSK3β), indicating GSK3β activation and subsequent phosphorylation of C-MYC at T58 ( Fig. 5A ). Similarly, WEE1 knockdown using siRNA in the same cell lines produced comparable effects, showing elevated p-T58 C-MYC and decreased total C-MYC along with reduced p-S9 GSK3β, confirming that WEE1 depletion activates GSK3β and enhances C-MYC phosphorylation ( Fig. 5B ). To further confirm this regulatory link, we performed proximity ligation assays (PLA) to visualize GSK3β–C-MYC interactions at the single-cell level. Following MK-1775 treatment, the number of red fluorescent PLA foci representing GSK3β–C-MYC complexes was markedly increased, demonstrating enhanced co-localization and interaction between the two proteins ( Fig. 5C ). Next, we constructed the kinase-dead WEE1 mutant (K328A) overexpressing plasmid to determine whether the kinase activity of WEE1 is essential for regulating C-MYC stability. By comparing the effects of wild-type and kinase-inactive WEE1 expressed at similar levels, we aimed to distinguish whether C-MYC stabilization depends on WEE1’s catalytic function or occurs through a kinase-independent mechanism. overexpression of WEE1 protein coding sequence (WEE1-CDS) in OE33, SK-GT4, and OE19 cell lines resulted in substantial induction of C-MYC protein, consistent with inhibition of GSK3β activity measuring by increased p-S9 GSK3β after WEE1 overexpression ( Fig. 5D ). In contrast, expression of a kinase-dead WEE1 mutant (K328A) failed to stabilize C-MYC and instead led to a noticeable decrease in its basal levels ( Fig. 5E ). This is consistent with a dominant-negative effect, whereby the mutant competes with endogenous WEE1, thereby failing to inhibit GSK3β and subsequently promoting C-MYC degradation. This further confirms the critical importance of WEE1’s kinase activity in regulating C-MYC stability. Both wild-type and kinase-dead WEE1 proteins were expressed at comparable levels, indicating that the observed differences were not due to unequal expression ( Fig. 5E ). While wild-type WEE1 overexpression led to a marked increase in p-CDC2 (Y15), consistent with its functional kinase activity, the K328A mutant failed to induce CDC2 phosphorylation ( Fig. 5E ). Correspondingly, wild-type WEE1 significantly elevated C-MYC protein levels. In contrast, the kinase-dead mutant had no such effect ( Fig. 5E ). These findings clearly demonstrate that WEE1’s kinase activity is required to maintain CDC2 phosphorylation and promote C-MYC stabilization. To confirm the specificity of MK-1775 and rule out off-target effects, we overexpressed WEE1 (WEE1-CDS) in OE33 and SK-GT4 cells and subsequently treated them with MK-1775. While WEE1 overexpression stabilized C-MYC in the control cells, treatment with MK-1775 successfully reduced the stability of C-MYC despite WEE1 overexpression ( Supplementary Figure 4A & 4B ). To verify whether GSK3ß is a substrate for WEE1, we performed in vitro kinase assay using recombinant full length GSK3ß and increasing concentration of recombinant full length WEE1 while recombinant S100A4 protein was used as positive control. Immunoblot analysis using P-GSK3ß S9 antibody revealed that WEE1 was capable of directly phosphorylating GSK3ß in vitro ( Supplementary figure 4C ). Furthermore, GSK3ß inhibitor TWS 119 was able to rescue C-MYC from degradation induced by MK 1775 treatment, attesting the role of GSK3ß in promoting C-MYC degradation ( Supplementary figure 4D ). In summary, these results demonstrate that the inhibition or loss of WEE1 activates GSK3β, leading to the phosphorylation of C-MYC at T58 and promoting its ubiquitin–proteasome–mediated degradation. This establishes a mechanistic link between WEE1 activity and C-MYC stability in EAC cells.

sections.section: Wee1 Inhibition Compromises Drug Efflux By Suppressing The C-Myc-Abcc1 Axis
sections.text: To investigate the functional consequence of C-MYC activation in esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) and to determine whether WEE1 inhibition can counteract the effects of C-MYC overexpression, we examined the role of WEE1 in regulating the C-MYC–ABCC1 signaling pathway that contributes to chemoresistance. Previous studies [ 52 ] have shown that the overexpression of ATP-binding cassette (ABC) efflux transporters, such as P-glycoprotein (P-gp), multidrug resistance protein 1 (MRP1), and breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP), limits the intracellular accumulation of anticancer drugs. Among these, MRP1, encoded by the ABCC1 gene, is transcriptionally regulated by C-MYC in several C-MYC–driven tumors [ 41 ]. Overexpression of C-MYC can therefore enhance drug efflux and contribute to reduced therapeutic efficacy. To validate this potential mechanism in human EAC, we analyzed 5 normal esophageal and 80 gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma tissues using tissue microarray (TMA)–based co-immunofluorescence staining followed by quantification using CellProfiler. Both C-MYC and MRP1 were markedly elevated in adenocarcinoma tissues compared with normal esophagus, and their expression levels were positively correlated ( Fig. 6A – C ). Since WEE1 inhibition or knockdown reduced ABCC1 mRNA levels, as we found in Fig. 2 & 3 , we next examined the corresponding protein, MRP1, in OE33, FLO1, and SK-GT4 cells following WEE1 inhibition. Western blot analysis revealed that MK-1775 treatment decreased MRP1 expression along with C-MYC, suggesting that WEE1 inhibition suppresses the C-MYC–ABCC1 regulatory axis ( Fig. 6D ). To determine the phenotypic consequence of suppressing this drug efflux axis, we performed cell viability assays combining MK-1775 with standard-of-care chemotherapies. As expected, MK-1775 robustly synergized with both cisplatin and oxaliplatin, significantly reducing their IC50 values in OE33 and SK-GT4 cells ( Supplementary Figures 5C – 5F ). To rigorously validate this in a chemoresistant setting, we established an oxaliplatin-resistant OE33 cell line. Western blot analysis confirmed that these resistant cells inherently overexpressed WEE1, C-MYC, and MRP1 compared to parental OE33 cells ( Supplementary Figure 6A ). Crucially, targeted WEE1 inhibition with MK-1775 successfully re-sensitized these cells to oxaliplatin, resulting in a substantial reduction in the oxaliplatin IC50 ( Supplementary Figure 6B ). To study the functional effects on the MRP1 transporter, Rhodamine 123, a fluorescent substrate for MRP1, was used to directly assess the activity of the efflux membrane pump in live EAC cell lines, OE33 and SK-GT4. This assay enables us to directly measure the extrusion of Rhodamine 123 by living cells under physiological conditions. It can also determine the effect of candidate drugs that may inhibit or block the activity of this protein. OE33 and SK-GT4 cells were incubated with 0.25 μM Rhodamine 123 for 60 minutes, washed, and allowed to efflux the dye for 4 hours. Flow cytometry analysis revealed that intracellular retention of Rhodamine 123 was substantially higher in MK-1775–treated cells than in control cells, rising from 54.3% to 94.3% in OE33 and from 37.9% to 83.7% in SK-GT4 cells ( Fig. 6E – J ). Since C-MYC is a master transcriptional regulator of various stemness markers, we tested some of the markers such as CD 133, CD44, OCT 4 and Nanog known to be regulated by MYC. CD44 was consistently down regulated in WEE1 knock down and MK 1775 treated EAC cells ( Supplementary figure 6C & 6D ). Together, these findings demonstrate that WEE1 inhibition impairs C-MYC–driven MRP1 expression and function, thereby compromising drug efflux and promoting intracellular drug retention. This suggests that targeting WEE1 can effectively counteract C-MYC–mediated chemoresistance in EAC.

sections.section: Wee1 Inhibitor Mk-1775 Synergizes With Panobinostat In Vitro And In Vivo
sections.text: To identify potential therapeutic agents that synergize with MK-1775, we performed a high-throughput drug screen using a library of 892 FDA-approved compounds from Cayman Chemical in the relatively MK-1775-resistant OE19 cell line, which has the highest MK-1775 IC50s ( Supplementary Figure 5A ). The screening included four treatment groups: control, MK-1775 alone (0.5 μM), FDA-approved drug alone (1 μM), and the combination. After 96 hours of treatment, cell viability was measured using the ATP-Glo assay, and synergy was quantified using Bliss synergy score analysis. Compounds that showed a statistically significant decrease in cell viability in the combination group compared with either MK-1775 or the drug alone (P < 0.05) were considered positive hits. This first round identified 21 candidate compounds with more than a fourfold increase in cytotoxicity under combination treatment ( Fig. 7A ). These candidates were further validated in FLO1 and SK-GT4 cell lines in a second-round screen to identify the most synergistic agents ( Fig. 7B ). Among these, Panobinostat, a histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor, emerged as the most potent synergistic compound, displaying strong synthetic lethality at nanomolar concentrations across all four EAC cell lines tested ( Supplementary Figure 5B , Fig. 7C ). To evaluate the efficacy of the MK-1775 and Panobinostat combination in vitro, we assessed apoptosis using Annexin V and Sytox Red dual staining in OE33 and OE19 cells. Flow cytometric analysis revealed a significant increase in the Annexin V-positive apoptotic fraction in the combination treatment group compared with either single-agent treatment ( Fig. 7D , E , G , H ). Consistent with this observation, Western blot analysis showed elevated levels of apoptotic markers, including cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved PARP, in the combination group relative to the single-agent treatments ( Fig. 7F and 7I ). Furthermore, combination treatment for 72 hours markedly induced a greater decrease in the growth of patient-derived xenograft (PDX) derived human EAC organoids compared with single treatment, confirming the enhanced cytotoxicity of the dual therapy ( Fig. 8A and 8B ). To further determine the therapeutic potential of this combination in vivo, we established human EAC PDX-derived xenografts and treated mice with MK-1775, Panobinostat, or the combination for four weeks. Consistent with our in vitro findings, the MK-1775/Panobinostat combination significantly suppressed tumor growth compared with the single-agent group, demonstrating a clear synergistic antitumor effect ( Fig. 8C ). Western blot analysis of tumor lysates revealed increased cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved PARP levels in the combination group, confirming enhanced intratumoral apoptosis ( Fig. 8D ). Immunofluorescence analysis of PDX tumor sections further validated the effectiveness of WEE1 inhibition and a pronounced reduction in C-MYC expression following combination treatment. Additionally, tumor proliferation was substantially reduced, as evidenced by a decrease in Ki67-positive tumor cells ( Fig. 8E and 8F ). Together, these findings demonstrate that Panobinostat synergizes with the WEE1 inhibitor MK-1775 to induce robust apoptosis, inhibit tumor proliferation, and suppress EAC growth both in vitro and in vivo. These results provide strong preclinical evidence supporting the MK-1775/Panobinostat combination as a promising therapeutic strategy for esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Esophageal adenocarcinoma remains a highly lethal malignancy with limited therapeutic options and poor long-term survival rates [ 53 ]. Despite efforts to improve treatment outcomes through multimodal approaches, most patients relapse due to therapy resistance and distant metastasis [ 54 ]. Therefore, there is an urgent need to identify actionable vulnerabilities in EAC that can be therapeutically exploited. MYC activation is a frequent event in EAC, commonly driven by gene amplification, transcriptional upregulation, and dysregulation of associated networks such as the MYC/MAX/MAD pathway [ 55 ]. Known mechanisms include MYC gene amplification, altered regulation by antagonistic proteins (MAD, MXI1), and activation through oncogenic pathways including STAT3 signaling [ 56 ]. Functionally, MYC promotes cellular proliferation, growth factor independence, metabolic reprogramming, and self-renewal of esophageal epithelial cells, all of which contribute to tumor growth and progression in EAC [ 57 , 58 ]. In this study, we demonstrate that the G2/M checkpoint kinase WEE1 is abnormally overexpressed in human EAC cells, promoting C-MYC stability and transcriptional activity in EAC. Furthermore, we demonstrate that pharmacological inhibition of WEE1 disrupts this axis, leading to C-MYC protein degradation. Furthermore, the first FDA-approved drug synergy screening with the WEE1 inhibitor in EAC was performed, identifying a synergistic therapeutic interaction between WEE1 inhibitor MK-1775 and the HDAC inhibitor Panobinostat, both in vitro and in vivo , establishing a rational combination strategy for targeting C-MYC-driven EAC. Firstly, we found that WEE1 is overexpressed in the cytosol of EAC cells in human EAC tissue samples and in EAC cell lines. This supports our hypothesis that WEE1 is involved in more than just cell cycle regulation in EAC. This tumor-specific correlation suggested a functional interaction between WEE1 and C-MYC in the context of malignancy, which has never been reported before in EAC. Our hypothesis was further confirmed by GSEA in EAC tissue samples from five different datasets, including TCGA, indicating that WEE1 is involved in activating or maintaining the oncogenic functions of C-MYC in EAC, a tumor type characterized by frequent TP53 mutations and C-MYC upregulation [ 55 ]. Further immunostaining and Western blot analysis in EAC cell lines and tissues confirmed that both proteins are highly expressed, with WEE1 surprisingly predominantly localized in the cytoplasm, consistent with its non-canonical novel function of C-MYC activation. To dissect the functional significance of this correlation, we employed both pharmacological (MK-1775) and genetic (siRNA) inhibition of WEE1 in multiple EAC cell lines. This dual approach not only suppressed the phosphorylation of CDC2, thereby validating WEE1 inhibition, but also resulted in consistent reductions in C-MYC protein levels and C-MYC-driven transcriptional activity. Importantly, we utilized a well-characterized C-MYC-responsive 4XEMS luciferase reporter system and qRT-PCR of established C-MYC targets, such as MNT, CDK4, and ABCC1 [ 59 ], to demonstrate the loss of C-MYC transcriptional activity, thereby reinforcing the specificity and robustness of our findings. Importantly, we confirmed the specificity of these interventions and ruled out potential off-target effects. A second, independent pool of WEE1 siRNA successfully recapitulated the reduction in C-MYC levels, validating our genetic knockdown approach. Furthermore, a pharmacological rescue experiment revealed that while WEE1 overexpression stabilized C-MYC, concomitant treatment with MK-1775 abrogated this effect. This demonstrates that the observed destabilization of C-MYC is directly dependent on the specific pharmacological inhibition of WEE1 kinase activity. Another piece of evidence supporting our findings is that WEE1 knockdown in EAC cells significantly decreases C-MYC downstream signaling, as measured by GSEA. All these data support our hypothesis that WEE1 activates C-MYC in EAC cells. A key mechanistic question we addressed was whether WEE1 modulates C-MYC abundance by regulating its protein degradation. Because MYC overexpression in many cancers arises primarily from increased protein stability rather than elevated transcription, understanding how WEE1 influences MYC degradation is critical to uncovering mechanisms that sustain oncogenic MYC activity [ 60 , 61 ]. CHX chase assays demonstrated that WEE1 inhibition accelerates C-MYC turnover, reducing its half-life. Furthermore, MG132, a proteasome inhibitor, reversed the decrease in C-MYC protein induced by WEE1 inhibition. These experiments provided strong evidence that WEE1 maintains C-MYC protein stability by preventing its proteasome-mediated degradation. Interestingly, our clinical datasets revealed elevated MYC mRNA levels, along with WEE1, in EAC tumors. To reconcile this with our findings on protein stability, we evaluated MYC transcript levels following WEE1 inhibition and knockdown. We observed a significant decrease in MYC mRNA in SK-GT4 cells, though this was not consistent across all cell lines, as OE33 cells did not show a similar reduction. This suggests that while WEE1 consistently and predominantly regulates C-MYC through post-translational stabilization across our EAC models, its influence on MYC transcription is highly cell-line dependent. Therefore, transcriptional upregulation and post-translational stabilization likely act cooperatively in certain cellular contexts to sustain oncogenic C-MYC activity in EAC. We then interrogated the upstream signaling responsible for C-MYC degradation, focusing on GSK3β, which phosphorylates C-MYC at threonine 58 (T58), a key event triggering its ubiquitination by FBXW7 [ 51 ]. Upon WEE1 inhibition, we observed decreased GSK3β phosphorylation at serine 9, indicating activation, and a corresponding increase in C-MYC phosphorylation at T58. Both immunoblot and proximity ligation assays validated this sequence of molecular events. Furthermore, our in vivo ubiquitination assay demonstrated that C-MYC poly-ubiquitination is significantly enhanced in MK-1775-treated cells. This provides direct biochemical evidence that WEE1 stabilizes C-MYC by shielding it from ubiquitin-proteasome-mediated degradation, likely through the GSK3β–FBXW7 axis. In the present report, we demonstrate a marked reduction in ABCC1 mRNA in MK1775 and WEE1-siRNA-treated EAC cells. The inability of the kinase-dead WEE1 mutant (K328A) to stabilize C-MYC, despite comparable expression levels to the wild-type protein, indicates that WEE1’s regulatory effect on C-MYC is not due to scaffolding or non-catalytic interactions but instead requires its enzymatic function. The observation that wild-type WEE1 increased both p-CDC2 (Y15) and C-MYC levels suggests that WEE1’s kinase-dependent signaling contributes to maintaining cellular conditions that prevent GSK3β-mediated phosphorylation and proteasomal degradation of C-MYC. Conversely, loss of WEE1 kinase activity appears to disrupt this regulatory balance, leading to activation of GSK3β and accelerated C-MYC degradation. In vitro kinase assay using recombinant GSK3ß and increasing concentration of recombinant WEE1 suggested that WEE1 is capable of directly phosphorylating GSK3ß at the inhibitory site S9. Together, these findings reveal that WEE1’s kinase activity plays a key role in stabilizing oncogenic C-MYC in EAC. The multidrug resistance protein MRP1 is one of the major indicators of chemotherapy resistance [ 62 ] and known to be over-expressed by oxaliplatin resistance hepatocellular carcinoma cells [ 63 ]. A similar study has revealed a relationship between MYC and ABCC1 in childhood Neuroblastoma [ 64 ]. ABCC1 correlates with poor prognosis and drug resistance in a variety of cancers [ 65 ]. IF analysis of MRP1 and C-MYC in the esophageal-gastric junction TMA revealed a positive association between the proteins. Additionally, kinetic analysis of MRP1 substrate Rhodamine 123 efflux was performed to quantify drug transport in live OE33 and SK-GT4 cell lines. Rhodamine 123 has been shown to interact directly and specifically with MRP1 [ 66 ] therefore, we took advantage of the intrinsic fluorescence of Rhodamine 123 to determine drug efflux through flow cytometry. The fluorescence signal recorded in MK-1775-treated cells was markedly higher than that observed in untreated control cells, due to reduced MRP1. The functional significance of this impaired drug efflux was phenotypically confirmed by our observation that MK-1775 not only synergized with standard platinum-based chemotherapies but also successfully re-sensitized an established oxaliplatin-resistant EAC cell line that exhibited baseline overexpression of the WEE1-MYC-MRP1 axis. It is well-established that WEE1 inhibitors primarily reverse chemoresistance by disrupting the G2/M checkpoint, thereby forcing cancer cells with DNA damage to bypass repair and undergo premature mitosis and cell death. While this canonical mechanism is undoubtedly a primary driver of chemosensitization, our findings uncover a parallel, previously unrecognized vulnerability in MYC-driven cancers. By demonstrating that WEE1 inhibition also suppresses the C-MYC-ABCC1 axis and reduces MRP1-mediated drug efflux, we highlight a dual-action therapeutic benefit. Therefore, targeting the aberrant cytoplasmic pool of WEE1 not only forces mitotic catastrophe but has the beneficial secondary effect of enhancing intracellular drug retention, making highly aggressive EAC cells intrinsically more susceptible to conventional chemotherapies. The above findings support the notion that WEE1-mediated C-MYC reduction not only compromises its oncogenic programs but additionally sensitizes cancer cells to the effect of chemotherapeutic drugs. Furthermore, MYC is a master transcription factor for various stemness markers, which are critical drivers of tumor recurrence and therapy evasion. We demonstrate that WEE1 depletion or inhibition significantly reduces the protein levels of the cancer stem cell marker CD44, a glycoprotein involved in tumor progression and metastasis [ 67 – 71 ], as a direct result of the decline in C-MYC. Consistent with the downregulation of both MRP1 and CD44, we found that MK-1775 synergistically enhanced the cytotoxicity of standard-of-care chemotherapeutics, such as cisplatin and oxaliplatin, and successfully re-sensitized oxaliplatin-resistant EAC cells. While re-sensitizing tumors to conventional chemotherapy is a critical benefit of WEE1 inhibition, translating this into a viable clinical strategy presents distinct challenges. C-MYC has long been considered an ‘undruggable’ target due to its nuclear localization and lack of enzymatic activity [ 57 ]. Suppressing its upstream regulator, WEE1, offers a promising indirect approach; however, single-agent WEE1 inhibition has frequently been insufficient to achieve optimal anti-cancer effects in clinical trials [ 13 ], often constrained by dose-limiting toxicities. Acknowledging that successful combination therapies often operate through independent or parallel pathways to achieve synthetic lethality, we sought to build upon our mechanistic foundation by identifying an FDA-approved synergistic partner for MK-1775. This translational effort led to the identification of the HDAC inhibitor Panobinostat. Although Panobinostat’s synergistic induction of apoptosis likely functions independently of the WEE1-MYC degradation axis, identifying this FDA-approved partner is critical for developing a highly translatable, rational combination strategy that maximizes cytotoxicity against MYC-driven EAC while potentially reducing normal tissue toxicity. Mechanistically, HDAC inhibitors like Panobinostat are known to induce chromatin remodeling and modulate transcriptional programs associated with apoptosis and DNA damage responses [ 72 ]. Our data show that the combination of MK-1775 and Panobinostat significantly enhances apoptosis, as demonstrated by Annexin V staining and increased levels of cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved PARP. The combination treatment also reduced proliferation in 3D organoid cultures and inhibited tumor growth, extending survival in patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. These in vivo findings further validate the clinical relevance of the WEE1–C-MYC axis and the efficacy of combination therapy. Taken together, this study provides the first comprehensive evidence that WEE1 activates C-MYC oncogenic signaling in EAC by inhibiting GSK3β-mediated protein degradation. Our experimental design, combining patient data analysis, molecular dissection in cell lines, reporter assays, proteasomal and kinase mechanistic studies, and in vivo efficacy testing, provides a logically structured and scientifically rigorous demonstration of the WEE1–C-MYC relationship. This integrated approach effectively addresses our central hypothesis and highlights WEE1 inhibition as a viable strategy to target C-MYC indirectly. Moreover, the combination of MK-1775 and Panobinostat offers a clinically translatable approach for improving therapeutic outcomes in EAC. Future work will be needed to explore biomarkers predictive of response to this combination and to determine whether similar regulatory interactions exist in other C-MYC-driven cancers. Nonetheless, these findings open a promising avenue for rational drug combinations that exploit synthetic vulnerabilities in C-MYC-addicted tumors.
